summary: This Perspective reviews the emergence and evolution of the digital-analog quantum paradigm over the past decade, which combines native analog interactions from quantum platforms (acting on tens to hundreds of qubits) with digital single- and two-qubit gates to enable scalable, versatile quantum simulation and computing without requiring quantum error correction in the near term. Implementations across trapped ions, superconducting circuits, and Rydberg atoms have demonstrated record numbers of qubits for useful computations, establishing digital-analog techniques as the de facto standard for current large-scale quantum experiments.
motivation: Purely digital approaches suffer from error accumulation scaling poorly beyond ~10 qubits, while purely analog approaches lack universality and versatility; the digital-analog paradigm was developed to pragmatically combine the scalable many-qubit entangling blocks of native platform interactions with the versatility of discrete gates, enabling near-term quantum advantage without full error correction overhead.
method: The approach interleaves large analog blocks (time evolution under native Hamiltonians like Ising or XY models) with digital single-qubit rotations and occasional two-qubit gates, generalizing Lie-Trotter-Suzuki decomposition by replacing short digital timesteps with long analog evolution times; this framework is applied across trapped ion chains, superconducting qubit arrays, and Rydberg atom arrays.
result: Recent experiments achieve $>50$ qubits for useful quantum simulations in superconducting circuits and trapped ions, and up to hundreds of Rydberg atoms in cold atoms platforms; digital-analog quantum supremacy has been proven theoretically, and the paradigm enables quantum advantage on current quantum annealers and digital-analog hybrid devices without requiring fault-tolerant error correction.
